routes.description: Establish that Christianity lacks proportionate rational warrant by applying consistent evidential standards to its supernatural claims and showing that revelation, doctrine, and theistic explanations do not overcome available objections or alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christianity's distinctive claims require support not supplied by transmitted testimony, religious experience, or worldview comparison, while unclear revelation, contested doctrine, and unresolved counterevidence prevent those claims from being rationally justified.

motionBridge.description: Connect inadequate support for Christianity's distinctive claims and material undefeated objections to the conclusion that Christianity is not rationally warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require evidence proportionate to supernatural claims and apply the same justificatory standard to Christianity and incompatible religions.
Show that indirect historical transmission, disputed revelation, and resurrection premises do not establish Christianity's conclusions about Jesus or God.
Provide non-theistic accounts of morality and fallible reasoning sufficient to resist claims that Christianity uniquely grounds value or rational inference.
Relate unclear communication, moral disagreement, and troubling scriptural claims to the expected attributes of an omnipotent and loving God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish atheism from materialism and determinism so that objections to those positions do not by themselves establish Christian rationality.
Explain how testing and verification can support rational inquiry despite uncertainty about evolved cognition.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity is rational through a cumulative comparative case in which theism accounts for cosmic order, objective value, and reason, while historical considerations and experience provide specifically Christian warrant.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian belief can rest on good evidence without requiring certainty, Christianity supplies a coherent comparative explanation of reason and morality, and the resurrection and revelation claims remain historically and intellectually defensible against the principal objections.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative explanatory and historical case to the conclusion that accepting Christianity can be rational.

centralBridges.description: Show that fine-tuning and mathematical intelligibility are better explained by purposive mind than by unguided alternatives.
Show that Christian theism can ground truth-directed reason, human dignity, moral obligation, and responsibility more coherently than reductive naturalism.
Establish sufficiently reliable access to early Christian claims and defend resurrection as an explanation of the relevant historical facts.
Explain how interpretive method, divine purposes, and qualified evidential access can answer objections from difficult scripture, disagreement, and uneven revelation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Define rationality so that good-faith disagreement and lack of certainty do not automatically make Christian belief irrational.
Integrate personal experience and Christianity's account of meaning and hope as supporting considerations within the wider case.

sections.title: Evidential Standards, Revelation, and Access
sections.rationale: Determines what rational belief requires, whether one standard is applied across religions, and whether disagreement, personal experience, unequal access, and the chosen mode of revelation bear on Christian warrant.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Intelligibility, and Theistic Explanation
sections.rationale: Tests whether fine-tuning and mathematical order materially support purposive mind, including the force of probability qualifications and the challenge that religious interpretation follows external scientific correction.

sections.title: Morality, Human Dignity, and Scriptural Coherence
sections.rationale: Covers rival accounts of moral obligation and human value together with disagreement, justice and mercy, and difficult biblical narratives that test Christianity's claimed moral coherence.

sections.title: Reason, Freedom, Evolution, and Naturalism
sections.rationale: Addresses whether determined or evolved cognition can remain rationally trustworthy, whether theism supplies a better foundation for reason, and whether atheism is properly identified with the naturalistic positions under challenge.

sections.title: Resurrection, Testimony, and Christian-Specific Inference
sections.rationale: Examines the principal bridge from general theism to Christianity: the reliability of early testimony, the explanatory case for resurrection, and whether reported miracles entail the claimed identity and authority of Jesus.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Rational belief requires good reasons, but reasonable people may assess the available evidence differently, so disagreement alone does not make either Christian or atheist belief irrational.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Justin immediately before this uninterrupted first-person opening address.

response.rationale: This is a constructive definition of rational belief and disagreement, so it has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes a usable standard, though the phrase personally valid remains underexplained.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable and expressly qualified, but personally valid reasons is not sharply distinguished from good reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that disagreement can coexist with rationality fits the limited conceptual support and expressly avoids declaring atheists irrational.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between disagreement and irrationality is coherent, with one bounded ambiguity concerning what makes reasons personally valid.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual point is plausible, but no account is supplied for separating genuinely good reasons from merely sincere reasons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary rational-disagreement bridge by defining a non-certainty standard for rational belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is assessed closely enough to support a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt requires good reasons, permits rational Christian and atheist belief, and denies that disagreement itself establishes irrationality.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Christian belief may be rationally grounded in an undefeated personal experience, while objective investigation can also provide intellectual support for Christianity.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person autobiographical account continues within Justin's uninterrupted opening speech.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers experiential and investigative grounds for belief and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a recognizable experiential warrant, but objective investigation is only announced in the selected evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experience claim and undefeated-defeater condition are clear, bounded, and expressly distinguished from objective evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker claims possible justification absent a compelling defeater, not proof, which matches the autobiographical and epistemic support offered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The undefeated-experience inference is intelligible, though it leaves implicit why religious experience initially deserves epistemic trust.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies changed lives and absence of defeaters but provides no verification, reliability comparison, or alternative explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the experience-and-cumulative-fit subsidiary bridge by supplying an explicit experiential basis for Christian belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a positive experiential position without developing a competing interpretation for assessment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says subjective experience can justify belief until a compelling reason defeats trust in that experience.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Life-permitting fine-tuning and the mathematical intelligibility of nature make more explanatory sense if a purposive mind stands behind the universe than if both are unguided coincidences.
moves.attributionBasis: Justin explicitly numbers this as his first constructive consideration and develops it without a speaker change.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a comparative theistic explanation and has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances two related explanatory considerations, though rival explanations receive little treatment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is clear, but the relevant explanatory standard and range of unguided alternatives remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying purposive mind makes more sense is comparative rather than certain, but the selected support does not establish the comparison against serious rivals.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning and mathematical intelligibility may have impersonal physical or selection-based explanations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling unguided reality luck does not exhaust the available non-theistic explanatory alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A purposive mind is a relevant candidate explanation, but the bridge from intelligibility and fine-tuning to comparative superiority is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Wigner is invoked and the phenomena are described, yet no likelihood comparison, parameter evidence, or serious rival analysis is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic-explanation bridge through both fine-tuning and mathematical intelligibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move contrasts mind mainly with coincidence or luck and does not engage stronger impersonal or selection-based alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes mathematical predictability, Wigner's formulation, and rejects coincidence in favor of a mind behind nature.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Christianity grounds objective human dignity and moral obligation in humanity's creation in God's image and Christ's sacrifice, where material facts alone do not yield moral oughts.
moves.attributionBasis: Justin marks this as his second argument and sustains the first-person Christian comparison throughout the window.

response.rationale: This is a constructive comparative account of dignity and obligation and thus has no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a direct Christian grounding claim, but compresses its criticism of atheistic alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding claim is recoverable, but objective value, atheism, and material facts range across distinct positions without sufficient qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that atheism fails while Christianity explains value is stronger than the brief scriptural account and absent rival comparison warrant.

charity.alternative: Non-theistic moral realism or naturalistic accounts may ground dignity without deriving ought directly from bare material description.
charity.decisiveQualification: Atheism alone does not entail a single reductive moral ontology or denial of objective value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Creation and sacrifice can function as internal grounding claims, but the comparative inference relies on an underdefined atheism and a compressed ought bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biblical claims support the internal Christian account, but the failure of non-theistic accounts is asserted rather than comparatively demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central reason-and-morality bridge by addressing dignity, value, and moral grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats atheism as failing to account for value without addressing live non-theistic realist or constructivist alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts alleged atheistic failure with the image of God and Christ's sacrifice as sources of human dignity.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: If beliefs are fixed wholly by non-rational material causes, confidence in reasoning is undermined, whereas creation by God can make genuine freedom and rational deliberation intelligible.
moves.attributionBasis: Justin identifies Stephen by name, describes the opposing worldview, and presents the theistic alternative in one continuous argument.

response.rationale: This constructive argument offers a theistic foundation for freedom and reason, with no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents the central self-defeat challenge and theistic alternative, but leaves major bridges implicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but non-rational causes, closed system, freedom, and reason shift across causal and epistemic senses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling a guarantor the only way out asserts necessity without excluding compatibilist freedom or truth-tracking natural cognition.

charity.alternative: Determined or materially caused cognition can still respond reliably to reasons and track truth without libertarian choice.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal determination does not by itself show that a belief lacks rational relations or epistemic reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference moves too quickly from causal determination to epistemic defeat and then from God to guaranteed freedom and rational reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The self-defeat claim and divine solution are asserted without evidence about cognition's reliability or comparison with naturalistic accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central reason-and-morality bridge by making God the proposed foundation of trustworthy deliberation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument largely equates material determination with non-rationality and does not preserve the strongest compatibilist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the naturalistic position self-defeating, says a guarantor is required, and identifies God with freedom and reason.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Jesus's crucifixion, the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and the emergence of the early church are collectively best explained by the resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Justin transitions explicitly from generic theism to Jesus and completes the historical argument before summarizing his speech.

response.rationale: This constructive historical inference introduces the resurrection case and has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a structured set of explananda, although the comparative explanatory work remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical facts and best-explanation conclusion are identifiable, but evidential independence and the comparison class remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Best explanation carries strong comparative force, while the excerpt lists claims without defending their reliability or testing alternatives.

charity.alternative: The reported facts may have mixed historical status and admit combinations of grief experience, legend, error, or social development.
charity.decisiveQualification: A best-explanation inference requires reliable, sufficiently independent facts and comparison with serious non-resurrection hypotheses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed facts are relevant to resurrection, but their conjunction does not establish comparative superiority without explicit explanatory criteria.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific historical claims are enumerated, yet their sources, independence, disputed status, and alternative explanations are not defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central resurrection-history bridge through a clearly identified historical best-explanation argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a cumulative list but does not engage the strongest natural or mixed explanations of that list.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists crucifixion, empty tomb, appearances, conversions, and early church growth as the resurrection explananda.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Christian acceptance of evolution followed correction by overwhelming scientific evidence rather than clear foresight in Genesis, weakening revelation as an independent guide to explanations of nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen continues his audience-poll argument in the same uninterrupted opening address and explicitly discusses Christianity's historical response.

components.text: Explain why fine-tuning and mathematical intelligibility favor purposive mind over unguided alternatives.

response.rationale: The history of Christian accommodation to evolution bears on revelation's independence, but it does not contact the fine-tuning move's decisive comparative inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it supplies concrete contrary material about revelation but leaves the targeted explanatory argument untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical criticism is clear, but claims about most Christians and Christianity as a whole are broad and unqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence supports significant historical correction, but the sweeping claim about Christianity being dragged requires broader documentation.

charity.alternative: Genesis may not have been intended as a scientific account, and Christian traditions contained nonliteral readings before modern evolution.
charity.decisiveQualification: Later scientific correction still bears on revelation's independent clarity even if literalism was never universal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Scientific correction can weaken claims of clear independent revelation, though it does not directly undermine a separate fine-tuning inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete historical pattern is identified, but claims about majority belief, persecution, and institutional change are not documented or delimited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the central objection-resilience bridge by challenging revelation's clarity and independence from external correction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move emphasizes historic literalism but omits the decisive qualification that nonliteral Christian interpretation predates modern science.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts historical Genesis-based creation belief with Christianity's later accommodation under overwhelming scientific evidence.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evidential standards permissive enough to rationalize Christianity also rationalize incompatible religions, while healthier standards reject those claims and Christianity-only standards constitute special pleading.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen explicitly announces the topic at hand and lays out a structured three-alternative evidential argument in his opening speech.

components.text: Show why undefeated personal experience can justify Christianity rather than incompatible religious conclusions under the same standard.
Distinguish rational disagreement from standards permissive enough to validate mutually inconsistent religious claims.

response.rationale: The trilemma directly challenges the permissiveness and consistency of both experiential justification and the stated rational-disagreement standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive consistency problem but does not establish that every available Christian standard fits its trilemma.

precisionFindings.rationale: The trilemma is recoverable, but lower standards and rationalizing a religion need more precise epistemic and scope conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The exhaustive framing overstates what follows because rational permissibility of incompatible beliefs need not violate non-contradiction between propositions themselves.

charity.alternative: Different people may rationally hold incompatible beliefs on different evidence without both propositions being true.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic rationality is not identical to truth, and permissibility need not affirm a contradiction within one person's beliefs.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The special-pleading concern is legitimate, but the trilemma conflates rational permissibility with truth and does not establish exhaustiveness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a clear consistency challenge but no representative comparison showing that the Christian standard equally warrants incompatible religions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central proportionate-evidence bridge by demanding consistent evidential treatment across religions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invokes non-contradiction as though rational permission for different agents entailed jointly asserting incompatible propositions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that lowering standards rationalizes incompatible religions and appeals to non-contradiction against that result.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: An omnipotent and loving God could communicate Christianity clearly to everyone, so widespread unbelief, doctrinal disagreement, and reliance on poor indirect transmission count against the claimed God.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen frames the argument explicitly as a consequence of the Christian worldview attributed to Justin and the audience, then develops it continuously.

components.text: Explain why uneven personal experience and indirect transmission remain expected if an omnipotent loving God wants Christian belief.
Explain why widespread disagreement is merely rational diversity rather than evidence against clear divine communication.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges experiential and disagreement-based defenses by deriving an expectation of clearer universal communication from divine attributes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive clarity demand but leaves possible divine purposes for noncoercive or uneven revelation untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The expectation is clear, but all-loving, convince, and everyone require qualification concerning divine aims, freedom, and responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that a loving God already would convince everyone is stronger than warranted without excluding competing divine purposes or constraints.

charity.alternative: A loving God may value noncoercive response, moral development, or mediated human participation rather than irresistible universal disclosure.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those purposes must still explain severe and apparently arbitrary disparities in access to salvific information.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expectation from omnipotence and love is intelligible, but the inference to universal immediate conviction needs an additional premise about divine aims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Widespread disagreement and indirect transmission are concrete considerations, but their distribution and incompatibility with divine purposes are not demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-coherence-objections bridge by linking unclear communication to claimed divine attributes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move highlights unequal access forcefully but does not engage the strongest purpose-based account of mediated or noncoercive revelation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says an omnipotent loving God could and would convince everyone, contrasting that expectation with indirect ancient transmission.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Rationality consists in aligning beliefs and actions with the available reasons and evidence, rather than in freely choosing which beliefs one holds.
moves.attributionBasis: The response directly answers Brierley's request for an account of rationality and develops Woodford's distinction between rationality and truth.

components.text: Show that causally determined belief cannot count as rational unless a person freely chooses that belief.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference's failure by separating rational responsiveness to reasons and evidence from voluntary choice of beliefs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly contacts the decisive freedom-to-rationality inference and states a replacement criterion for rationality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between truth, rationality, evidence, reasons, and voluntary belief is stated clearly enough for evaluation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The offered account is framed as a definition and correspondence standard, without claiming certainty that cognition always succeeds.

charity.alternative: The guarantor argument may concern truth-tracking reliability rather than merely voluntary choice over individual beliefs.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defining rationality without choice does not by itself establish the reliability of the cognitive process producing reasons and evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction coherently blocks the inference from lack of belief choice to irrationality, with reliability left as a separate question.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinctions are well articulated, though the proposed standard's truth-tracking properties are not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central reason-and-morality bridge by rejecting the claimed necessity of libertarian choice for rationality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly defeats the free-choice requirement but does not fully address the stronger evolutionary or truth-tracking version.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes truth from rationality and defines rationality as correspondence between beliefs, actions, evidence, and reasons.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Moral systems can arise from shared aversion to suffering, biologically grounded interests, and cooperative social rules even if moral wrongness is not metaphysically ultimate.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford answers the moral challenge in the first person, contrasting religious interpretation with his naturalistic account of human preferences and cooperation.

components.text: Provide a non-theistic account of moral reasons, social rules, and human interests sufficient to resist unique Christian grounding.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the comparative moral-grounding demand through shared interests, aversion to suffering, biology, and cooperation, while conceding no ultimate metaphysical wrongness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it supplies a substantive practical account but does not fully answer objective dignity or categorical obligation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical account is recoverable, though morality shifts between preferences, genetic dispositions, cooperation, and right-and-wrong rules.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a sufficient naturalistic possibility rather than metaphysical certainty and acknowledges its non-ultimate status.

charity.alternative: The Christian challenge concerns objective categorical obligation and intrinsic dignity, not merely cooperative rules serving shared preferences.
charity.decisiveQualification: A practical naturalistic morality can resist claims of social incoherence while leaving metaphysical objectivity unanswered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared interests and cooperation can coherently generate practical norms, although the transition from evolved desires to right and wrong is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account draws on familiar biological and cooperative mechanisms but gives no concrete evidence or defense against exploitation and disagreement.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central naturalistic-coherence bridge by offering a non-theistic account of morality and cooperation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes interpretive subjectivity and offers a rival account, but only partially meets the strongest objective-grounding demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds preferences and aversions in human biology and begins deriving interpersonal right-and-wrong rules from shared life.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: The biblical punishment of David through the death of his innocent child conflicts with the claimed existence of an omnipotent and omnibenevolent God.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford introduces the Samuel passage, summarizes the punishment it depicts, and expressly formulates the resulting challenge to God's attributes.

response.rationale: This constructive moral objection introduces a biblical counterexample and therefore has no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies a specific text and a direct conflict with the claimed divine attributes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged conflict is clearly recoverable, though the reading assumes the narrative directly attributes punitive purpose to the child's death.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The quoted passage strongly supports a moral problem, but a strict logical incompatibility requires further premises about justice and divine purposes.

charity.alternative: The narrative may describe judgment within a culturally situated text without endorsing a simple rule that innocent suffering is morally good.
charity.decisiveQualification: The text still explicitly connects the child's death to David's deed, leaving the punitive moral problem intact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Punishing a parent through an innocent child's death creates a direct prima facie tension with omnibenevolence, though not a complete contradiction unaided.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific scriptural passage is quoted and directly supports the claimed punitive connection, with broader textual context remaining unexamined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central divine-coherence-objections bridge through a specific morally troubling scriptural narrative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection relies on the passage's express punitive connection while allowing that broader interpretive context could qualify its force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes Nathan linking the child's death to David's deed and describes the child as innocent punishment of the father.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Morally difficult Old Testament narratives need not defeat rational Christianity because they are partial and culturally situated revelations whose interpretation is governed by the fuller revelation of God in Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley answers Woodford's scriptural objection by challenging its moral basis, qualifying the passage's interpretation, and presenting Jesus as his hermeneutical lens.

components.text: Explain how the child's punitive death can be reconciled with the goodness of an omnipotent and omnibenevolent God.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the objection by offering a Christ-centered, partial-revelation interpretive framework, but it does not resolve the specific child's-death moral conflict.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts a secondary interpretive component while leaving the decisive justice question substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hermeneutical proposal is clear, but culturally situated and partial revelation do not specify which narrative claims are corrected or retained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest need-not-defeat conclusion fits the availability of a Christological interpretive lens, though its application remains incomplete.

charity.alternative: The objection concerns the morality of the narrated divine act even if later revelation supplies a fuller picture of God.
charity.decisiveQualification: A later interpretive lens must explain whether the act occurred, was misattributed, or can be morally justified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A progressive-revelation hermeneutic is coherent, but no explicit bridge shows how Jesus changes the moral assessment of this particular act.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Hebrews and the Christological lens support the interpretive method internally, but its application to the cited passage is not demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central objection-resilience bridge by proposing a method for handling difficult Old Testament narratives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the difficult narrative but substitutes a general hermeneutic without answering its strongest specific moral demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls Old Testament material partial revelation and makes Jesus the final interpretive lens for evaluating it.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Christian supernatural claims require evidence proportionate to their extraordinary character, and transmitted testimony, apparent wonders, and potentially altered texts do not supply that evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted closing-statement passage follows Woodford's explicit transition and consistently uses his first-person hypothetical examples.

components.text: Supply evidence proportionate to resurrection and defend transmitted testimony as reliable enough for the extraordinary conclusion.
Show why subjective experience can carry adequate weight for specifically supernatural Christian claims.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the sufficiency of testimony and experience for extraordinary claims, although the selected excerpt mainly develops the governing standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive evidential demand but only compresses its application to the resurrection's particular sources.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proportionality standard and its application to supernatural claims are recoverable and illustrated through differing ordinary claim types.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The standard is well calibrated, but the categorical insufficiency of transmitted evidence needs fuller source-specific comparison than appears here.

charity.alternative: Cumulative testimony and historical evidence may jointly make a rare event more probable than each item considered alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative force depends on source reliability, independence, prior probability, and comparison with ordinary alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The principle that evidential demand rises with claim extraordinariness is coherently illustrated, with exact probabilistic application left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy clarifies the warrant, but the conclusion about Christian texts requires more direct analysis of reliability, alteration, and dependence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central revelation-and-resurrection-gap bridge by challenging the adequacy of testimony for supernatural conclusions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument allows likelihood updating by trustworthiness and focuses fairly on whether the cumulative evidence is proportionate.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states proportional evidence and illustrates Bayesian-like updating by claim type and prior speaker trustworthiness.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Even provisionally granting Jesus's virgin birth and resurrection would not logically entail that Jesus is God's son, leaving Christianity's identity inference unsupported.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Woodford's uninterrupted closing statement and explicitly develops his announced second objection to Christianity.

components.text: Show that establishing resurrection would warrant the further specifically Christian conclusion about Jesus's divine identity.

response.rationale: The reply grants the miraculous premises arguendo and identifies the missing entailment from virgin birth or resurrection to divine sonship.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it isolates the decisive Christian-specific inference and states exactly what would remain unsupported even after concession.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional concession and limited conclusion are explicit, stable, and readily separable from the independent evidence dispute.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The narrow claim is that the conclusion does not logically follow from those premises alone, which the explicit provisional concession supports.

charity.alternative: Resurrection may support divinity when combined with Jesus's prior claims, religious context, and a broader cumulative case.
charity.decisiveQualification: The two miraculous events alone still do not deductively identify their cause or establish divine sonship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure cleanly demonstrates underdetermination: extraordinary events alone do not identify a unique divine status or cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical point needs little external evidence, though assessing the broader Christian inference would require Jesus's claims and contextual evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central revelation-and-resurrection-gap bridge by exposing a missing Christian-specific identity inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately limits its attack to the entailment and does not claim that no broader cumulative identity argument could exist.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grants virgin birth and resurrection for argument's sake and denies that divine sonship follows from them.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Textual criticism, early documentary proximity, indications of eyewitness testimony, and Paul's preservation of early traditions provide substantially reliable access to first-century Christian claims.
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley explicitly turns to textual transmission and continues the same audience answer until the moderator invites a brief response from Woodford.

components.text: Show that Christian testimony is textually recoverable, early, and connected to eyewitness or preserved early tradition.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the transmission challenge with textual criticism, temporal proximity, claimed eyewitness indications, and Pauline tradition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive access and reliability component but does not establish independence or supernatural sufficiency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The access claim is clear, but extremely close, lots of indications, and pretty good idea are comparative terms without defined baselines.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The materials support historical access in principle, but substantial reliability is stronger than the undocumented comparisons and indications supplied.

charity.alternative: Early texts can preserve first-century claims while remaining anonymous, dependent, theologically shaped, or mistaken about miracles.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical access to claims is not equivalent to independent eyewitness confirmation or proof that the claims are true.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Textual recoverability, proximity, eyewitness indications, and early traditions are relevant to access, though not sufficient by themselves for truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific evidence categories are named, but dates, documents, textual variants, eyewitness markers, and comparison standards are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central revelation-and-resurrection-gap bridge by defending reliable access to early Christian claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply meets the access objection but tends to move too quickly from early documents and indications to substantial reliability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes early documentary proximity, textual access, internal eyewitness indications, and Paul's preservation of earlier material.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: Although a fine-tuning tolerance cannot be translated straightforwardly into an ordinary probability, the extreme precision of the life-permitting range still calls for explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange identifies the challenged statistic as Brierley's earlier claim, and this first-person answer concedes limitations in his own prior probability presentation.

components.text: Answer the claim that Christian interpretation of nature followed external scientific correction rather than clear revelation.

response.rationale: The probability qualification bears on fine-tuning methodology but does not contact the earlier Genesis-and-evolution criticism's decisive revelation demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it improves an adjacent fine-tuning claim but leaves the targeted history-of-revelation objection unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between ordinary probability and tolerance level is explicit, while the remaining explanatory claim is clearly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker concedes the probabilistic criticism and retains only the more modest claim that extreme life-permitting precision needs explanation.

charity.alternative: A narrow life-permitting range may be striking without licensing a known probability distribution or design inference.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting ordinary probability language does not remove the need to compare design with physical necessity, selection, or multiverse accounts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The correction cleanly distinguishes tolerance from event probability and validly retains an explanatory question without claiming a numerical chance.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The concession improves the warrant, though the degree of fine-tuning and comparison among explanations remain unsupported in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central theistic-explanation bridge by refining rather than abandoning the fine-tuning consideration.

representationalCharity.rationale: The concession accurately preserves the strongest methodological objection while retaining a limited explanatory question.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes that repeated-dice probability differs from a constant's tolerance, then retains the need to explain life-permitting precision.

moves.speaker: Justin Brierley
moves.proposition: If evolution selects cognition primarily for survival rather than truth, naturalism lacks an adequate basis for trusting the beliefs generated by evolved cognition.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly characterizes the preceding answer and invokes Plantinga, matching Justin's earlier argument from reason and naturalism.

components.text: Explain why reasons-responsive rationality remains trustworthy if evolved cognition is selected primarily for survival rather than truth.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the remaining reliability issue after the freedom response by arguing that survival-directed evolution may undercut trust in cognition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive truth-tracking component but does not establish that survival and true belief are sufficiently disconnected.

precisionFindings.rationale: The defeater is recoverable, but evolved beliefs and primarily directed at survival are generalized across cognitive domains without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts that naturalism is undercut without showing that adaptive cognition is generally unreliable or that true representation lacks survival value.

charity.alternative: Accurate environmental representation often promotes survival, while social correction and verification can improve domain-specific reliability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolution need not optimize abstract truth directly for many truth-tracking capacities to be adaptively reliable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A reliability defeater is relevant, but the inference depends on an unsupported separation between survival fitness and truth-tracking cognition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Plantinga's name and the survival-selection premise are supplied, but no evidence establishes low reliability across the beliefs being challenged.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary verification-under-fallibility bridge by challenging the trustworthiness of evolved cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move frames survival and truth as too sharply opposed and does not engage their substantial possible correlation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that evolution selects survival-directed rather than true beliefs and claims this undercuts naturalistic trust in cognition.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Uncertainty about evolved cognition is unavoidable but manageable through verification, and it does not justify adopting a more appealing theistic worldview.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker addresses Justin by name, defends the naturalistic worldview in the first person, and is answered by Justin within the final row.

components.text: Explain how fallible evolved cognition can earn rational trust through verification despite lacking certainty.
Show why epistemic discomfort or uncertainty does not warrant inferring a divine guarantor of reason.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the defeater with verification and fallibilism and rejects the inference from uncertainty or appeal to a more comfortable worldview.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive verification component but does not explain how verification escapes reliance on the same cognition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fallibilist conclusion is clear, but verification is left broad and its procedures and independence are unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply expressly accepts uncertainty and makes the limited claim that discomfort does not license a more appealing worldview.

charity.alternative: Verification itself uses evolved cognition, so it may not answer a global defeater without some independent reliability account.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cross-checking, prediction, replication, and error correction can improve reliability even when no cognitive process is infallible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Fallible cognition and verification are compatible, and uncertainty does not entail theism, though the anti-circular reliability bridge is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Verification is a relevant mechanism, but no examples, success criteria, or evidence of independent error correction are provided.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary verification-under-fallibility bridge by explaining how inquiry can proceed without certainty.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies verification but does not develop the strongest noncircular account of why those methods earn trust.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts evolved cognitive limits, invokes verification, and denies that uncertainty justifies choosing a more appealing worldview.
